text: A skill is a reusable set of instructions that tells co-pilot how to perform a specific type of task. So instead of repeating the same guidance every time, you can package it into a skill and then reuse when you need it. A custom co-pilot skill is typically built around a file called skill.md. That file starts with some basic information about the skill, like the name and a description of what the skill does and where it should be used. Below are the instructions co-pilot should follow. Effective skill instructions include the typical co-do elements, so who should co-pilot act like, what results are you trying to achieve, what should it do and not do, and what should the finished result look like. But because a skill is designed for repeatable work, you can go further when the job requires it by defining things like the steps that co-pilot should follow and maybe in which order, which tools or resources it should use and any checks it should perform before returning the results. So a simple way to think about it is that a good prompt gives co-pilot strong instructions for the work in front of you, but a skill makes those instructions reusable and can add the process and resources needed to perform that work consistently. Now where you find skills depends on the co-pilot experience that you are using. For this lesson I'll focus on using a custom skill inside PowerPoint. So I'm going to start by opening up the co-pilot panel in PowerPoint and from here I can get to skills in two ways. I can select the three-dot menu in the top right corner and choose Manage Plugins and Skills, or from the prompt box I can select plus, choose skills, and then select Manage Plugins and Skills. Custom skills are stored in designated locations in OneDrive. So for this demo I'm going to use a file-based approach and upload an existing skill into PowerPoint. So here's a folder for my leadership update skill and inside it is that skill.md file. If I open it you can see the skill name and the description followed by the instructions that define how I want co-pilot to prepare, in this case a leadership update. So now I'm going to go into PowerPoint, open up co-pilot, I select Manage Plugins and Skills, and here I can see Microsoft's built-in skills for PowerPoint as well as a custom skills area where I can add my own. For this demo I already have my skill file so I'll choose to upload an existing skill. I select the leadership update skill and then edit. And once the skill is available I can return to the prompt box, select plus, choose skills, and select leadership update. And then I can ask, turn this project information into three slides for the leadership team. Co-pilot now uses the presentation as source material and applies the skills instructions to decide what to prioritize, how to structure the update, and how concise that update should be. At this point I can review the output, confirm that the information is accurate and complete, and make any adjustments before using or sharing the slides. The result is a leadership-ready summary organized around the key developments, risks, decisions, and next steps defined in the skill. Now keep in mind that a skill available in PowerPoint may not automatically appear in Excel for example. If you want to reuse the same skill across applications, you may need to add or copy it into the location that each co-pilot experience expects. The availability of skills and the exact interface may also vary by the application that you're using, your license, and your organization's settings.
